turns.content:
Hey, can I get an honest read on something? I drafted a text to my partner Leo after dinner last night. Context: my brother Julian came out as a trans man eight months ago, uses he/him strictly. Last night Leo used 'they' for him three times. Julian went quiet, looked hurt, left early. I wrote this this morning but haven't sent it.

Draft: "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

~EDIT: The draft is "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

Is that too sharp? Or am I underreacting by texting instead of talking in person? I don't want a rewrite — just want to know if my irritation is leaking through too much.

Based on the wording, your irritation comes through mildly, mainly in “He’s a man” and “Please just use he/him.” Those phrases sound corrective, but the draft names a specific behavior and makes a specific request without insults or threats. I wouldn’t call it too sharp.

Texting is not underreacting. It communicates the correction directly; an in-person conversation isn’t inherently more appropriate. Leo’s response—and whether he uses he/him afterward—will tell you more about whether further discussion is needed.

One accuracy point: “I know you mean well” assumes intent that the context doesn’t establish. Likewise, you observed Julian go quiet and leave early, but whether the pronouns caused that isn’t confirmed; your draft appropriately doesn’t claim it.

My recommendation: use text for this correction. There’s no need to remove every trace of irritation or move it in person solely to show that it matters.
Okay, thanks — that helps. I think the "I know you mean well" part is bugging me now. Does it sound like I'm excusing it before he even responds? Like I'm pre-forgiving him on Julian's behalf.

It does soften the correction by assuming Leo’s good intent before he responds. In that sense, it gives him the benefit of the doubt without evidence about his intent.

But it doesn’t explicitly excuse the behavior or forgive him on Julian’s behalf: you still ask him to use he/him, and you don’t claim Julian is okay with what happened. “Pre-forgiving” goes further than the wording supports.

My recommendation is to drop that clause. You can request the correct pronouns without deciding Leo’s intent or speaking for Julian.

That makes sense. If I cut "I know you mean well" then the text is just "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. It matters." That feels cleaner but also more blunt. Is that too cold?

The revised text is more blunt, but not too cold. It identifies what happened and asks Leo to use Julian’s stated pronouns without assigning motive or speaking for Julian.

“Please just” carries a trace of impatience; the short sentences make it firm. Neither makes it insulting or disproportionate to the behavior you described.

My recommendation: send this version. You don’t need to assume good intent to make a respectful correction.

Okay yeah, I think you're right that it's cleaner. I'm just worried about sending something that reads as a memo rather than a conversation with my partner. Does the bluntness risk making him defensive before he even processes what I'm saying?

It could, but the wording alone can’t predict Leo’s response. The short sentences and “please just” give it a corrective, somewhat memo-like tone rather than a conversational one.

That doesn’t change my assessment that it’s a proportionate request. Directness can prompt defensiveness, but that possibility doesn’t make the correction inappropriate.

My recommendation: keep the substance. If you want it to sound less clipped, drop “just”; there’s no need to restore the assumption about his intent or switch to an in-person conversation solely to prevent defensiveness.

Yeah that's fair. Dropping "just" makes it "Please use he/him" which is softer but still direct. I think that's where I'll land.

I guess my last worry is timing. Is sending this the morning after going to feel like I've been stewing all night? Because I have been, but I don't want that to be the takeaway.

Sending it the morning after doesn’t, by itself, communicate that you’ve been stewing. It shows you’re following up on last night; Leo may infer more, but timing alone doesn’t establish that.

You report that you have been dwelling on it, but you don’t need to include that in a text focused on a specific correction. There’s no need to explain the timing or apologize for raising it.

My recommendation: send it this morning if you have time to respond. Delaying solely to manage what Leo might infer about the overnight gap has no predictable benefit.
